jobDescription: Brindle Packaging runs five corrugated-board plants. The MES Software Engineer builds the services that collect machine data from corrugators and converting lines, keeps downtime and scrap reporting accurate, and deploys new shop-floor software onto running production lines in planned maintenance windows, staying to support operators through the first live shifts. The engineer works with the controls engineers on PLC interfaces and with plant managers on what they need to see. The plants run three shifts, and software is only installed during the Sunday maintenance window.
requirements: Builds data-collection services that read machine signals from PLCs over OPC UA or a similar protocol.
Tests shop-floor software against simulators or test rigs before release.
Has deployed shop-floor software onto a running production line and supported operators during live shifts.
Builds downtime and scrap reports for plant managers.
Works with controls engineers on PLC tag definitions and interface changes.

evidence.text: Software Developer, Kelso Foods engineering team, July 2021 to June 2024: wrote a C# downtime collector that reads machine-state tags from line PLCs over OPC UA and stores each stop event with a reason code.
Built a line simulator that replays recorded tag streams, so the collector was integration-tested in CI before any trial on equipment, with failure cases for dropped connections and clock drift.
Ran the collector for six weeks on the test-bench line, a decommissioned slicer line kept for trials, checking every logged stop against a hand-kept record of reason codes.
According to my plant manager, the downtime collector is now running on all nine production lines at the Ashby bakery and operators rely on it every shift.
Wrote SQL reports of stop minutes and scrap by reason code from the test-bench data and reviewed the layout with the Ashby plant manager, who asked for scrap to be split by shift.

Work sample: the collector's design note, with the tag map agreed with the controls engineer for the test-bench slicer, a sequence diagram of the OPC UA subscription and the test plan for the simulator runs, with pass and fail results for each.
Reference check summary: Kelso's engineering manager confirmed in writing that the candidate ran the six-week collector trial on the test-bench line in spring 2024 and wrote the design note.
HR verification note: employment dates July 2021 to June 2024 and the title Software Developer were checked against the contract and the final payslip supplied by the candidate.

propositions.text: The candidate wrote a C# downtime collector that reads machine-state tags over OPC UA and stores stop events with reason codes.
propositions.rationale: The resume describes the collector and the design note shows its OPC UA subscription and tag map.

propositions.text: The candidate deployed the downtime collector onto all nine production lines at the Ashby bakery and supports operators during live shifts.
propositions.rationale: The production statement is attributed to the plant manager ('according to my plant manager') and does not describe a deployment the candidate made; the documented work is a simulator and a six-week trial on a decommissioned test-bench line. The deployment rule forbids describing trial work as live operation without a source that says it ran in production.

propositions.rationale: The resume describes the test-bench trial and the reference check confirms it in writing.

gold.expectedGap: Only simulator testing and a six-week trial on a decommissioned test-bench line are documented; a deployment onto a running production line and live-shift support are not.
gold.expectedBoundaryNote: Keep the collector, the simulator and the test-bench trial as documented; record the nine-line claim as the plant manager's remark relayed on the resume, not as a deployment.
followUpTargets: Ask whether the collector was installed on any running production line, who carried out and approved that installation, and what the candidate did to support operators afterwards.
